routes.description: Defend Catholic theism by combining universally sufficient grace with providentially differentiated access, meaningful creaturely agency, and a deprivation account of original sin and suffering.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if grace remains genuinely available to everyone while unequal belief, rejection, inherited disorder, and suffering can arise without contradicting divine goodness or justice.

motionBridge.description: Grace, providence, and creaturely agency must jointly render the disputed phenomena compatible with Catholic theism.

centralBridges.description: Everyone must receive grace sufficient to begin a path toward conversion and salvation despite unequal historical mediation.
Persistent nonbelief and damnation must remain explicable through responsible creaturely refusal rather than divine exclusion.
Original sin must explain inherited disorder as deprivation of gratuitous gifts without assigning descendants personal ancestral guilt.
Temporal development, questioning, and suffering must be capable of serving a larger providential process of receptivity.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Religious geography must be assessed through culturally mediated testimony, obstacles, and indirect institutional effects.
Genesis must support the relevant theological claims without requiring literalistic reliance on every narrative mechanic.

routes.description: Challenge Catholic theism by arguing that religious geography, sincere nonbelief, hell, inherited deprivation, and unexplained suffering conflict with universal divine love and fair providence.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if these phenomena are more naturally expected without Catholic theism or if the proposed appeals to grace, agency, and providence leave the central moral and evidential conflicts unresolved.

motionBridge.description: The combined evidential and moral conflicts must count against Catholic theism rather than merely identify unexplained details.

centralBridges.description: Uneven religious geography must support cultural production more strongly than universally available divine relationship.
Sincere involuntary nonbelief must conflict with a willing and able God's desire for relationship and salvation.
Eternal loss must not rest fairly on ignorance, impaired reasoning, or contingently unavailable evidence.
Present deprivation and suffering must lack a just basis if the ancestral act was deceived or not personally chosen.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Contingent encounters and life-ending events must expose tension between providential intervention, equal access, and freedom.
The treatment of Job must bear on whether unexplained suffering is compatible with divine love and compassion.

sectionSelections.title: Religious Geography and Universal Access
sectionSelections.rationale: This issue connects the universal availability claimed for grace and relationship with the culturally uneven distribution of belief and conversion opportunities.

proSelections.proposition: Christian commitments hold that salvation, the Gospel, and relationship with Christ are available to everyone through ordinary human life.
Everyone receives sufficient initial grace, although revelation and testimony are mediated with differing historical and cultural thickness.

conSelections.proposition: The geographic distribution of religious belief is better explained by human sociological transmission than by a God seeking relationship with everyone.
Religious geography makes conversion substantially harder for some, while culturally varying religions are expected if religions are human products.

sectionSelections.title: Sincere Nonbelief, Rejection, and Hell
sectionSelections.rationale: This issue determines whether persistent nonbelief and eternal loss can be grounded in responsible rejection when conviction is involuntary and evidence remains noncompelling.

proSelections.proposition: Persistent nonbelief can involve free rejection of offered graces, with salvation originating in grace and damnation in creaturely refusal.
Only direct vision of God's essence compels assent; lesser signs permit alternative construal, for which attention, ignorance, weakness, and desire can bear responsibility.

conSelections.proposition: A sincere seeker cannot choose conviction, so eternal consequences based on cognitive limitations or unpersuasive arguments create a hiddenness problem.
Someone fully understanding eternal suffering and the supreme good could not rationally reject salvation, leaving ignorance or impaired reasoning as the basis of damnation.

sectionSelections.title: Providence, Contingency, and Creaturely Agency
sectionSelections.rationale: This issue addresses whether temporally extended and recurrent grace reconciles providence with freedom when conversion opportunities depend on contingent events and may end abruptly.

proSelections.proposition: Human freedom is limited but meaningful, and revelation may be recognized across a life through patient interpretation and perseverance.
Providence supplies recurrent opportunities for grace rather than controlling one decisive event, while resistance and inherited disorder can obstruct their reception.

conSelections.proposition: A lifelong-journey account remains vulnerable because another person's free action can end a seeker's opportunity and fix an eternal outcome.
If salvation turns on contingent encounters it appears arbitrary, but divine arrangement of those encounters threatens freedom and leaves unequal intervention unexplained.

sectionSelections.title: Original Sin, Deprivation, and Responsibility
sectionSelections.rationale: This issue supplies the proposed source of disordered agency and suffering while testing whether ancestral choice can justly ground deprivation for later human beings.

proSelections.proposition: Original sin was the first rational creatures' rejection of gifted dependence on God, resulting in the loss of grace, integrated powers, immortality, and impassibility.
Original sin is inherited as human nature deprived of superadded grace rather than added personal guilt, with restoration remaining available through salvation.

conSelections.proposition: Inherited suffering is morally troubling because the first humans appear vulnerable, deceived, and possibly without the moral knowledge required for culpability.
Even treating oneself as represented by Adam does not justify condemnation when the initiating action resulted from deception by a uniquely intelligent evil agent.

sectionSelections.title: Divine Silence, Formation, and Suffering
sectionSelections.rationale: This issue tests whether prolonged silence and suffering can form receptivity to providential meaning or instead conflict with the love and compassion attributed to God.

proSelections.proposition: Persistent questioning can enlarge a person's capacity to recognize and receive an answer even when divine response initially consists of deeper questions.
Read canonically, divine questions can provoke insight needed for revelation, while suffering may create capacities for perceiving a larger providential story.

conSelections.proposition: Sustained theological study, worship attendance, attempted prayer, and openness to prayer can occur without any reported discernible divine response.
Job appears to portray God inflicting suffering for a wager and rebuking the sufferer for seeking explanation, conflicting with divine love and compassion.
